stories.headline: At Least 13 Killed in Explosion at Qatar's Largest Gas Facility
stories.summary:
An explosion at Qatar's Barzan gas supply facility in the Ras Laffan industrial zone killed at least 13 people and injured 66 others on Sunday night. The blast, which turned the Doha skyline orange and rattled windows across central Doha, was felt more than 70 kilometers away. Qatar's Energy Minister Saad Sherida al-Kaabi said the incident was a technical accident and not sabotage, and that the government had launched an investigation into the cause.

All those killed were nationals of India and Pakistan, according to officials. The facility had only been restarted two days before the explosion after being shut down since December 2025 for urgent maintenance, and also after suffering extensive damage from Iranian retaliatory strikes during the US-Israel conflict with Iran earlier this year.

Ras Laffan is the world's largest LNG export facility, and Qatar supplies roughly a fifth of the world's LNG. Al-Kaabi stated the explosion would not affect Qatar's overall export commitments, though he acknowledged it would be difficult to determine when operations at the affected facility would resume. The incident raises fresh concerns about energy supply stability at a facility already strained by recent geopolitical conflict.

QatarEnergy said emergency response teams were deployed immediately and the fire has been brought under control. The Indian Embassy in Doha said it was in close contact with Qatari authorities to assist affected families. An investigation into the cause of the blast is ongoing.

stories.headline: Federal Appeals Court Blocks Trump Administration's CFPB Staff Cuts
stories.summary:
A federal appeals court on Friday blocked the Trump administration from proceeding with immediate workforce reductions at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit returned the case to the district court level while rejecting the administration's request to resume the staff cuts in the interim.

The ruling is the latest legal setback in the administration's broader effort to dramatically downsize or dismantle the CFPB, an agency created after the 2008 financial crisis to oversee consumer lending and financial products. The administration has argued the bureau is constitutionally overreaching and wasteful; critics and Democratic lawmakers contend the gutting of the agency would strip protections from millions of consumers who rely on it to police mortgage lenders, debt collectors, and credit card companies.

Supporers of the CFPB argue the court's action preserves an agency that has returned billions of dollars to consumers through enforcement actions. Opponents of the bureau, including many Republican lawmakers and financial industry groups, say the CFPB operates with insufficient accountability to Congress and should be fundamentally restructured or defunded.

The case now returns to the district court for further proceedings. The legal battle is part of a series of ongoing judicial disputes over the Trump administration's efforts to reshape or reduce the size of federal regulatory agencies.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Reinstates Murder Conviction in Etan Patz Case
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court voted 6-3 on Monday to reinstate the murder conviction of Pedro Hernandez in the 1979 disappearance and killing of 6-year-old Etan Patz of New York City. The court reversed a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, which had overturned Hernandez's conviction on grounds that the trial judge gave an inadequate answer to a juror question about his confession. The three liberal justices dissented.

In an unsigned opinion, the court held that federal courts exceeded their authority under a 1996 law designed to limit federal oversight of state criminal trials. Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg had argued the appeals court overturned a solid conviction on a procedural technicality, calling the basis for reversal a 'slender reed' that disregarded five months of trial proceedings involving 66 witnesses.

Hernandez, 64, has been serving a sentence of 25 years to life. He had confessed to the crime under police questioning before being read his Miranda rights, and later repeated the confession on tape. His attorneys argued the confession was false and that Hernandez suffers from a mental illness that causes hallucinations. He was tried twice previously — the first trial ended in a mistrial in 2015, and the second resulted in conviction in 2017.

Etan Patz vanished on May 25, 1979, while walking to his school bus stop in lower Manhattan. His case became nationally significant — he was among the first missing children featured on milk cartons, and the anniversary of his disappearance became National Missing Children's Day. With the conviction reinstated, Hernandez will remain incarcerated under his existing sentence.

stories.headline: Update: Ebola Cases in Congo Surpass 1,000 as Kenya Minister Held in Contempt Over US-Funded Quarantine Facility
stories.summary:
Congo's Ministry of Health confirmed Sunday that cumulative confirmed Ebola cases in the ongoing outbreak have exceeded 1,000, with 1,003 confirmed infections and 254 deaths reported. The majority of cases are concentrated in the Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu provinces. Health workers have warned that overcrowded displacement camps and ongoing conflict are severely hampering contact-tracing efforts.

Separately, a Kenyan court on Monday found Health Minister Aden Duale in contempt of court for allowing construction to continue on a controversial US-funded Ebola quarantine facility in Nanyuki despite a court order halting the project. The 50-bed isolation center, intended to house American citizens suspected of contracting Ebola in the Congo outbreak, has drawn fierce opposition from local residents and medical unions. Three people have died in protests against the project.

The judge ruled that the government could not circumvent the court order by recharacterizing the construction as a solely Kenyan government project and stated that a court order 'is not an invitation to ingenuity — it is a command to be obeyed.' Duale is scheduled to be sentenced on Tuesday. Kenyan President William Ruto had publicly defended the quarantine site, calling it a humanitarian necessity.

The milestone of 1,000 confirmed cases deepens concerns about the trajectory of the outbreak, which has also spread to Uganda with 20 confirmed cases, most imported from Congo. The combination of a worsening outbreak and political and legal turmoil over the containment infrastructure underscores the challenges facing international public health efforts, complicated in part by cuts to USAID funding.

stories.headline: Update: Vance Holds Tense 80-Minute Session with Iranian Officials in Switzerland as Trump Threats Complicate Talks
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance, joined by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met Sunday with Iran's lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Obbuergen, Switzerland, for roughly 80 minutes of negotiations aimed at translating the recent U.S.-Iran interim deal into a durable agreement. The session grew fraught after President Trump posted a social media threat warning he would hit Iran "very hard again, only harder" if Tehran did not rein in Hezbollah in Lebanon. Iranian state media declared the talks had entered a "difficult phase" and said the delegation recessed following Trump's "insulting message," though an official with knowledge of the proceedings told the Associated Press the Iranian side had not signaled any intention to leave.

The core issues at stake are Iran's nuclear program, the status of the Strait of Hormuz, and the unfreezing of billions of dollars in Iranian assets — all within a 60-day negotiating window that carries sweeping implications for global energy markets and regional security. Iran has also insisted that the Lebanon conflict, where Israel is fighting Iranian-backed Hezbollah, be addressed before other matters. Trump's demand that Iran stop funding its proxies in Lebanon directly clashed with Tehran's sequencing priorities.

Qalibaf responded to Trump on social media, warning that Iranian armed forces were "prepared to respond in a different manner" and that the U.S. should "be careful about their statements." Pakistan and Qatar are serving as mediators and worked to keep the Iranian delegation at the table after the recess. As of Sunday evening, it was unclear when formal sessions would resume.

The episode illustrates the central tension in the negotiations: American officials, led by Vance, are pressing for a broad restructuring of U.S.-Iran relations, while Trump's public statements repeatedly undercut the diplomatic atmosphere his own team is trying to cultivate. Critics on both sides of the U.S. political spectrum have raised concerns — hawks worry the interim deal conceded too much to Tehran, while some Democrats and foreign-policy analysts argue Trump's erratic messaging endangers any lasting settlement.

stories.headline: Russian Troops Infiltrate Strategic Ukrainian City of Kostyantynivka, Threatening Donbas Corridor
stories.summary:
Russian forces have infiltrated the eastern Ukrainian city of Kostyantynivka and are attempting to encircle it, according to BBC reporting based on accounts from Ukrainian soldiers operating inside the city. The entire city is now effectively a "grey zone" with no clear controlling force, Ukrainian drone operators told the BBC — a situation Ukrainian officials have been reluctant to acknowledge publicly. If the city falls, Russian forces would have a direct path toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, Ukraine's last major strongholds in the east and key objectives in Moscow's broader campaign to seize the Donbas region.

Ukrainian Brigadier General Oleksandr Bakulin, commander of the 19th Corps defending the area, insisted the situation "remains under control" and denied that Russian troops had achieved any meaningful success. However, he acknowledged approximately 130 Russian soldiers are operating inside the city. A Ukrainian officer who spoke anonymously told BBC that Russian forces were "accumulating more and more soldiers" and that building-by-building urban warfare was making it extremely difficult to dislodge them.

Russia has adapted its tactics in the city, using infantry advances through urban cover to reduce exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks, while Russian drone crews have shifted their targeting priority toward Ukrainian drone launch sites rather than infantry. Ukrainian commanders say they have overall recaptured more territory this year than they have lost along the broader front line, but Kostyantynivka represents a potentially significant reversal in the east.

The battle comes as Russian-appointed authorities in Crimea separately suspended public fuel sales due to shortages stemming from Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on oil infrastructure. Kyiv has continued long-range strikes on refineries near Moscow and St. Petersburg in an effort to bring the costs of the war to Russian civilians far from the front.

stories.headline: Former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Dies at 100
stories.summary:
Alan Greenspan, who served as chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006 and shaped U.S. monetary policy across five presidencies, has died at the age of 100 from complications of Parkinson's disease. His wife, NBC News correspondent Andrea Mitchell, confirmed the death in a statement calling him "a giant of a man who helped shape the US economy for decades under presidents of both parties, but was always honest in acknowledging his mistakes."

Greenspan presided over the longest sustained period of U.S. economic growth in a generation, guiding the country through the 1987 stock market crash, the dot-com boom, and the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. His approach to monetary policy — characterized by analytical rigor and deliberate opacity in public communication — became so influential that financial markets and media worldwide parsed his every word for signals about interest rates and economic direction.

The Federal Reserve issued a statement saying Greenspan's policies and economic thinking "left a lasting mark on this institution, on the broader field of economics, and on the country," crediting him with helping establish the central bank's credibility as one of its most important assets. Critics, however, have long argued that his preference for deregulation and easy credit helped inflate the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s and laid groundwork for the subprime mortgage crisis of 2008 — a charge Greenspan himself partially acknowledged in congressional testimony after the financial collapse.

Born in New York City in 1926, Greenspan studied clarinet at Juilliard and toured with a jazz band before turning to economics at New York University, where he became a committed free-market thinker influenced by philosopher Ayn Rand. He served as an economic adviser to President Nixon and later as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Ford before President Reagan appointed him to lead the Fed in 1987.

stories.headline: Three Students Killed in School Shooting at Philippine High School; Suspects Aged 14 and 15
stories.summary:
Three students were killed and at least six others injured when two teenage classmates opened fire inside a classroom at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City in the central Philippines on Monday. Police identified the suspects as a 14-year-old and a 15-year-old who investigators believe were motivated by a grudge over bullying. One suspect was arrested near the scene shortly after the attack; the second surrendered to authorities later in the day.

The pair were armed with a .38 caliber revolver and a 9mm pistol, the latter of which belonged to a relative of one suspect — a serving policewoman who has since been taken into custody. Philippine National Police spokesman Colonel Allen Rae Co said approximately 40 spent shell casings were recovered from the classroom. Three students were shot and wounded, while four more were hurt in the rush to flee.

Officials said clear behavioral warning signs, including violent videos of one suspect firing a gun that were posted to social media, had gone undetected. "If anybody was able to monitor these red flags, this could have been prevented," Co told reporters, adding that neither school officials nor parents had flagged the behavior. The mother of one slain 15-year-old called for criminal charges against anyone who allowed the shooters access to firearms.

School shootings are exceptionally rare in the Philippines despite a broader pattern of gun violence in the country, which recorded nearly 5,000 gun violence cases nationwide in 2024 according to national police data. President Ferdinand Marcos's office said he was "saddened" by the attack, and the education ministry announced a joint review with police of school security protocols, anti-bullying policies, and student behavioral monitoring systems.

stories.headline: Update: US-Iran Post-War Talks Open in Switzerland With 'Encouraging Progress,' Lebanon Fighting Persists
stories.summary:
The first round of formal negotiations between the United States and Iran to finalize a post-war deal concluded in Lucerne, Switzerland, with mediators Qatar and Pakistan declaring "encouraging progress" and announcing agreement on a "roadmap towards reaching a final deal within 60 days." Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi cited "major progress" on ending the conflict in Lebanon, while the joint mediator statement said a communication line had been established to manage vessel passage through the Strait of Hormuz and a "de-confliction cell" created between the US, Iran, and Lebanon.

The negotiations follow a memorandum of understanding signed last week that committed both sides to ending fighting "on all fronts," lifting the US blockade, and launching a $300 billion reconstruction plan for Iran. Iran's lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf struck a defiant tone, dismissing Trump's threats to resume military action as signs of "desperation." Iran's supreme leader also publicly distanced himself from the deal, saying Trump signed it "out of desperation."

Despite the diplomatic activity, violence in Lebanon has continued. Israeli strikes have killed dozens of Lebanese civilians according to Beirut's health ministry, and Israel reported four of its own soldiers killed by Hezbollah. A new ceasefire was declared Friday but clashes have persisted, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisting Israeli forces would remain in southern Lebanon indefinitely. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected any Israeli military presence in the south.

The agreement remains contested on multiple fronts. Iran's shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz — announced Saturday though tracking data showed vessels still transiting — and the ongoing Lebanon fighting represent the first tests of the MoU's implementation. The US warned it would restart military action and reimpose the blockade if Iran does not abandon nuclear ambitions, while analysts on both sides are debating which party can more credibly claim victory from the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Meloni Feud Escalates as Italy's Prime Minister Fires Back Over Popularity and Base Access
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni publicly rebuked US President Donald Trump on Sunday, telling him to "focus on your own popularity" after Trump questioned her approval ratings and accused her of failing to support American efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The exchange marks a sharp deterioration in what had been one of the closer US-European bilateral relationships since Trump's return to office, with Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani cancelling a planned trip to Washington early next week.

The dispute escalated from a G7 summit earlier in the week, where Trump claimed in a phone interview with Italian broadcaster La7 that Meloni had "begged" him for a photo and that he "felt sorry for her." Meloni called the claim "senseless" and said she was "frankly stunned," adding that "neither I nor Italy ever beg." Trump on Saturday also accused Meloni of causing "a great logistical inconvenience" by barring the US from using Italian air facilities for military operations against Iran.

Meloni has defended Italy's position on base access as governed by standing bilateral agreements that "cannot be violated" while she is prime minister. She acknowledged publicly that being Trump's ally had not helped her domestic approval ratings. The Italian political spectrum largely rallied behind her, with opposition figures as well as coalition members expressing support for her pushback.

The feud reflects broader strains within the Western alliance over Trump's military campaign against Iran, which Italy did not support. The two leaders had previously clashed over Trump's criticism of Pope Leo XIV, which Meloni called "unacceptable." Meloni had been considered the European leader closest to Trump ideologically, having been the only European head of government to attend his inauguration in January 2025.

stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak Worsening in Congo as USAID Cuts Hamper Response
stories.summary:
An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is accelerating, health officials say, with no approved medicine or vaccine available for the current strain. The response has been complicated by the Trump administration's cuts to USAID, which had previously funded significant portions of outbreak detection, containment, and treatment infrastructure in the region.

The DRC has historically been the epicenter of Ebola outbreaks, and international funding and logistics support have been critical to containing previous surges. Health officials are warning that the reduction in US-backed resources is leaving response teams under-resourced at a moment of growing caseloads. The combination of an active outbreak with no approved therapeutic and diminished international support raises the prospect of wider regional spread.

The situation draws renewed attention to the broader consequences of the dismantling of USAID's global health programs, which critics say have left dangerous gaps in epidemic preparedness. Supporters of the cuts argue that foreign aid spending required reform and that recipient nations should build greater domestic capacity. The Ebola outbreak adds to a list of ongoing public health crises — including a prolonged measles outbreak in Utah — where advocates say federal health infrastructure reductions are having tangible effects.

stories.headline: France Puts Half Its Regions on Red Heat Alert as Temperatures Approach 43°C
stories.summary:
Forty-nine of France's 96 administrative regions were placed under red heat alerts Monday as a severe heatwave pushed temperatures toward 43°C (109°F) in Bordeaux and above 40°C across much of western France. An estimated 63 million people are affected in total, with orange alerts covering dozens of additional regions. French authorities closed 845 schools outright and allowed 1,800 others to release students early.

Three elderly residents of the Gironde region, aged between 80 and 95, died over the weekend partly due to the heat, authorities said. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist warned that many citizens would suffer during the week and urged people to monitor vulnerable relatives and neighbors. National rail operator SNCF asked vulnerable passengers to postpone travel, and several Paris metro lines reduced services due to the conditions.

Meteorologists at Météo-France described the event as "widespread, long-lasting and intense," with temperatures not expected to drop until the end of the week. The heatwave extends beyond France: Madrid is forecast to hit 39°C and Rome 37°C, while Belgium has cancelled peak-hour train services Monday and Tuesday. The extreme heat follows an alcohol ban at France's annual Fête de la Musique festival this past weekend, where large outdoor crowds gathered in already dangerous conditions.
